t: Create Grid With Exactly One Path
o: We must output any m x n grid of '.' and '#' whose right/down free-cell paths from (0,0) to (m-1,n-1) number exactly one. Since any valid grid is accepted, the easiest idea is to leave free only the cells of one chosen monotone path and block everything else — then exactly that path exists. Example outputs use staircases, but an L-shaped corridor (entire top row plus entire right column) works equally well and is trivial to build.
k: Blocking every non-path cell guarantees uniqueness regardless of which monotone path you pick.
An L-corridor (top row + last column) is a valid monotone path and needs only two filled patterns.

a.i: Make row 0 entirely free and column n-1 entirely free; set every other cell to '#'. The only free route is: walk right along row 0 to (0, n-1), then walk down column n-1 to (m-1, n-1). Any deviation hits a '#'. Handles n = 1 naturally (the whole grid is one free column).
s: Rows 1..m-1: '#' repeated n-1 times followed by '.'.
a.t: O(m * n) time to emit the grid cells; O(m * n) space for the output.
a.sp: O(m * n) — the returned grid itself.

a.i: By symmetry, the corridor can run down the first column and then right along the last row: column 0 free, row m-1 free, everything else blocked. This produces the unique path Down...Down then Right...Right. It shows the construction generalizes to any single monotone path whose complement is fully blocked.
s: Rows 0..m-2: '.' followed by '#' repeated n-1 times; last row all '.'.
a.t: O(m * n) time to build the grid; O(m * n) space.

w: Either construction is fine since any valid grid is accepted; prefer the L-corridor for simplicity. Edge cases: m = 1 or n = 1 collapses to a single free line, which still has exactly one path. Common mistake: leaving the whole grid free (many paths) or building a serpentine (not monotone, invalid under right/down moves). Follow-up: count the number of paths in a given grid (DP over free cells).
